tip: Loanwords usually don't change shape: πολλά λάικ (pollá láik) has no plural ending – λάικ (láik) stays the same however many you get.
English verbs usually join Greek with -άρω (-áro): μπλόκαρα (blókara) = I blocked. Also ποστάρω (postáro = post), σερφάρω (serfáro = surf).
Έγινε διάσημο (éyine dhiásimo) is literally 'became famous' and is the normal way to say a video went viral.
Μου τελείωσαν τα δεδομένα (mou telíosan ta dhedhoména) is literally 'the data ran out on me' – the data is the subject and you are the affected μου (mou).
Κλείνω (klíno) means 'close' and it is also the booking verb: έκλεισα εισιτήρια (éklisa isitíria) = I booked tickets. Tables and rooms get closed too.
Greek closes what English turns off: έκλεισα τις ειδοποιήσεις (éklisa tis idhopiísis) – κλείνω (klíno) works for lights, phones and sound too.
Μέσα (mésa) here means 'in it': the article had lies in it, with μέσα sitting at the end.
Μην (min) before a verb makes a 'don't' command: μην πιστεύεις (min pistévis) = don't believe.
Γεμίζω (yemízo) = fill up, and what fills it needs no preposition: γέμισε διαφημίσεις (yémise dhiafimísis) = filled up with ads.
Ανέβασα (anévasa) = 'I put up' – the same verb that uploads videos also raises speed: ανέβασα την ταχύτητα (anévasa tin takhítita).
Μεταγλώττιση (metaghlótisi) means dubbing; in Greece it is rare outside children's shows, so most things stay subtitled.
Βγάζω φωτογραφία (vgházo fotoghrafía) is literally 'I take out a photo' and is the everyday way to say take a photo.
Greek keeps files in an actual cloud: στο σύννεφο (sto sínefo) is the same word as the ones in the sky – no separate tech term.
Greek phones strike, they don't ring: χτυπάει (khtipái) is the hit verb – doorbells and alarm clocks χτυπάνε (khtipáne) too.
You answer to a call in Greek: απάντησα στην κλήση (apándisa stin klísi) – απαντάω (apandáo) normally takes σε (se) before the thing answered.
The line got cut: κόπηκε η γραμμή (kópike i ghramí) is the usual way to say a call dropped.
Πιο (pio) before an adjective means 'more', with no ending change; add the article and it becomes 'most': ο πιο στενός (o pio stenós) = the closest.
Κάναμε παρέα (káname paréa) is literally 'we made company' = we hung out; κάνω παρέα με (káno paréa me) is the everyday way to say you hang out with someone.
Λείπω (lípo) flips English 'miss': the missed person is the subject, so λείπεις στην παρέα (lípis stin paréa) is 'you are missing to the group' = the group misses you.
Γνωρίζω (ghnorízo) means 'know' and its past means 'met': τη γνώρισα (ti ghnórisa) = I met her, got to know her for the first time.
Στηρίζουμε ο ένας τον άλλον (stirízoume o énas ton álon) = we support one another – literally 'the one the other', the fixed way to say 'each other'.
Της (tis) before the verb means 'to her': της εμπιστεύομαι (tis embistévome) = I entrust to her, since Greek trusts things to a person.
Κρατάω (kratáo) means 'hold', and with a time span it means 'last': κρατάει είκοσι χρόνια (kratái íkosi khrónia) = it has lasted twenty years.
Από παιδιά (apó pedhiá) is literally 'from kids' and means since childhood: φίλοι από παιδιά (fíli apó pedhiá) = friends since we were kids.
Χαίρομαι (khérome) ends in -ομαι, a shape that often marks something done to you, but here it just means 'I'm glad'.
Περνάμε ωραία (pernáme oréa) is literally 'we pass nicely' = we have a good time. In Greek you pass the time well, you don't have it.
Σαν (san) = 'like' for resemblance: σαν αδερφή (san adherfí) = like a sister. For how something is done, Greek normally uses όπως (ópos).
Χέρι χέρι (khéri khéri) = hand in hand: the noun is simply doubled, with no article and no word for 'in'.
Μου αρέσει (mou arési) works backwards: the liked person is the subject, literally 'he pleases me', which is why the verb is not in the 'I' form.
Εδώ και δύο χρόνια (edhó ke dhío khrónia) = 'for two years now'. εδώ και with a time span and the present tense covers English 'have been ... for'.
